transcript:
This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Corva Coleman.
The Vatican says Pope Leo remains hospitalized in Rome.
He had surgery yesterday to remove part of his lung after doctors discovered cancer.
The Vatican said today the Ponte's recovery is progressing normally.
The Faculty Senate at Cornell University is set to meet today.
Piers will begin the process of voting no confidence in university leadership.
It's in response to an allegation of a gang rape on campus in 2024.
And Piers Alyssa Nadd warning reports from Ithaca, New York.
The university announced changes to campus policies, including banning fraternity parties
through the end of the year.
But faculty still intend to use today's meeting to begin the process of voting no confidence.
Anne Marie Brady is a member of the Faculty Senate who co-signed the motion.
There's a great sense of anger and, I think, also sadness.
We have lost confidence in the administration to effectively address sexual assault and
sexual harassment on campus.
Over the weekend, more than 200 faculty and staff signed a letter to students that said,
"This administration does not speak for us."
They say the university has failed to keep students safe and more change is needed.
Alyssa Nadd warning, NPR News, Ithaca, New York.
Trump says Taiwan is going to buy liquefied natural gas, or LNG, from the United States.
He says Taiwan will buy 30 percent of the gas from an Alaska pipeline over 20 years.
From Taipei, Jan Kamentin Brumby explains more about the purchase.
Taiwan's state-owned energy company says it will buy six million tons of Alaskan LNG every
year with production beginning as early as 2032.
The project would cut time and costs, allowing U.S. LNG to enter Asian markets without crossing
the Panama Canal or skirting around the Horn of Africa.
Taiwan's Premier Zhou Rongtai says the government is working to steady the island's supply
of energy.
Jan Kamentin Brumby reporting.
Have you ever walked into a mall where a friendly salesperson approaches you with a free sample
of skincare cream?
Well, an NPR investigation has found that what follows can cost customers thousands.
And Biers Monica Estatieva reports.
Mary Eckerd discovered the charges after his mother's bank account overdrew.
Mary Eckerd is one of the hundreds of customers NPR uncovered that had been hit with thousands
of dollars in charges from beauty stores in malls for purchases that they say they never
authorized, didn't want, and cannot return.
The stores are independently owned, but they all sell skincare products distributed by
the Mazal Group.
Based in California, the owner is from Israel.
The federal government was looking into Israeli-owned skincare stores a decade ago for immigration
violations.
NPR found evidence that visa fraud is still happening in those stores today.
Monica Estatieva, NPR News.
You're listening to NPR.
The government says consumer prices got worse last month.
They were up 3.7 percent compared to a year ago.
Much of the problem is higher gas costs, but there were huge increases for people buying
home heating oil.
Separately, the government says those who get Social Security will receive a benefit increase
of 3.6 percent in January.
That's an average of about $75 a month.
The AI company OpenAI says it fired an employee who allegedly planted a secret recording device
in an office.
NPR's John Ruich reports the FBI is on the case.
OpenAI says it discovered a sophisticated recording device hidden in an office and used
its models to analyze it and identify who put it there.
It says it has no indications that the individual accessed or took AI model weights, source
code or customer data.
The Department of Justice said in a statement the suspect was a Saudi national who was arrested
on Friday.
It said he worked at OpenAI for over a year.
The audio recording device was found plugged into the USB port on the back of a TV in an
executive conference room.
Closed circuit TV footage showed the suspect near the conference room on several occasions.
And search history on an AI chatbot account associated with his spouse included prompts
related to building an audio recorder and remote accessing the device.
John Ruich, NPR News.
A federal judge has ruled President Trump cannot ban news organizations from the White
House because he doesn't like their coverage.
The media outlets CNN, MS Now and Politico sued after Trump banned them from these companies.
This is NPR.

topics.text: Vatican says Pope Leo remains hospitalized in Rome after lung surgery for cancer
Cornell Faculty Senate to begin no-confidence vote over handling of 2024 gang rape allegation
Trump says Taiwan will buy 30 percent of Alaska LNG over 20 years
NPR investigation finds skincare store charges costing mall shoppers thousands in unauthorized purchases
US consumer prices rise 3.7 percent year over year, driven by gas and heating oil costs
Social Security recipients to get 3.6 percent benefit increase in January
OpenAI fires employee accused of hiding recording device in executive conference room; FBI involved
Federal judge rules Trump cannot ban CNN, MS Now and Politico from White House over coverage
